human_tolerance.notes: The most abundant landbird in North America, with a population of about 370 million; breeds in open farmland and urban areas, is not shy about nesting close to human habitations, and takes earthworms from lawns. It is also a common pest in North American fruit orchards.

phases.name: breeding
phases.note: One of the earliest birds to lay eggs, beginning to breed shortly after returning to its summer range. Males defend a breeding territory and are less social in summer. Nesting runs from 1.5-4.5 m above ground; a clutch of three to five cyan-coloured eggs is incubated by the female alone, hatching after 14 days with the chicks leaving a further two weeks later; a new nest is built for each brood.

phases.name: flocking
phases.note: On the winter grounds the birds assemble in large flocks at night, roosting in trees in secluded swamps or dense vegetation; the flocks break up during the day when the birds feed on fruits and berries in smaller groups.

phases.name: absent
phases.note: Almost the whole Canadian and Alaskan breeding population winters south of Canada, so the species is absent from most of Canada in mid-winter; the Pacific Coast wintering range described in the source is the partial exception, and 0.9 is an authored fraction for the share that leaves.

phases.name: territorial
phases.note: Regional note, a judgement rather than a cited statement: most of the species winters south of Canada, but the source says that robins 'occasionally overwinter in the northern part of the United States and southern Canada', and the Great Lakes and Appalachian highlands in the northern US are within that band, so this locale is treated as holding robins year-round.

vocalizations.description: A complex, almost continuous cheery carol of discrete units often repeated and spliced into a string with brief pauses, sung from a high perch in a tree. Among the first songbirds to sing as dawn rises, sometimes hours before, and last as evening sets in.
Calls used to signal a ground predator approaching, and a nest or another robin being directly threatened; robins also band together to drive a predator away.

taxonomy.note: GBIF backbone gives family Turdidae and authority Linnaeus, 1766; ITIS scientific-name search returns TSN 179759 with the same authority.

external.note: GBIF usageKey 9510564 from species/match; ITIS TSN 179759 from the ITIS scientific-name search; NCBI taxon id 9188, eBird code amerob and IUCN category least concern (Q211005) from Wikidata P685, P3444 and P141.

conservation.note: Wikidata P141 = least concern (Q211005); the Conservation status section gives an extensive range of about 16 million km2 and a population of about 370 million individuals.

range.note: 'The species breeds throughout most of North America, from Alaska and Canada southward to northern Florida and Mexico', wintering from Florida and the Gulf Coast to central Mexico and along the Pacific Coast. The Caribbean and Central American countries are from the vagrant records, which the source lists as Jamaica, Hispaniola, Puerto Rico and Belize; Greenland is from the vagrant record there.

traits.locomotion_modes.note: 'Robins forage primarily on the ground ... pouncing on them and then pulling them up' is a hop-and-walk ground gait, plus powered flight; the species also roosts in trees.

traits.nest_type.note: 'The nest is most commonly located 1.5-4.5 m above the ground in a dense bush or in a fork between two tree branches'; a cup of long coarse grass, twigs, paper and feathers, lined with smeared mud and cushioned with fine grass.

traits.perching.note: 'It usually sings from a high perch in a tree'; nests in bushes and branch forks and roosts in trees.

traits.senses.note: vision_color authored from the males' jet-black to grey head with white eye arcs and supercilia and the reddish-orange breast. hearing High from the species finding worms 'by sight (and sometimes by hearing)'. olfaction set Low, no sourced claim found.

traits.size_class.note: From mass_kg (0.0785 kg falls in the Small band, under 1 kg).

traits.mass_kg.note: EltonTraits BodyMass-Value 78.5 g and AVONET Mass 78.5 g agree exactly (both sourced to Dunning 2008) and sit within Wikipedia's stated ranges (males 72-94 g, females 59-91 g, species average about 77 g).

traits.mass_range_kg.note: Males 72-94 g and females 59-91 g; the narrower of the two sex ranges is used as the species range.

traits.length_m.note: Midpoint of 23 to 28 cm for the eastern subspecies T. m. migratorius.

traits.wingspan_m.note: Midpoint of 31 to 41 cm, 'with similar size ranges across all subspecies'.

traits.lifespan_y.note: 'The longest known lifespan of an American robin in the wild is 14 years; the average lifespan is about two years.' The average is recorded here, not the maximum.

traits.diet.note: EltonTraits Diet-Inv 50, Diet-Fruit 50. Wikipedia's Diet section gives a different split, 'around 40 percent small invertebrates ... and 60 percent wild and cultivated fruits and berries', but agrees on the character of the diet; the sourced EltonTraits fractions are used and Wikipedia's 40/60 noted here.

traits.social.note: Flock is the primary structure from 'on its winter grounds, it assembles in large flocks at night to roost in trees'; 'During the summer, males defend a breeding territory and are less social', so the flock size range is the winter-roost figure and 2 is the lower bound for a territorial pair. The upper bound of 100 is an authored figure for a large communal roost, since the source says 'large flocks' without a count.

traits.activity_pattern.note: 'The American robin is active mostly during the day, and on its winter grounds, it assembles in large flocks at night to roost' - diurnal by day, communal roost at night.

traits.defense.note: Authored: 'The adult's main predator is the domestic cat; other predators include hawks and snakes', and robins flee and hide from ground predators such as cats. The species also bands together to mob predators, which is a real but secondary response, so Flee is recorded as the main reaction.

traits.wariness.note: Judgement: 'The species is not shy about nesting close to human habitations' and it feeds on lawns, so a low value.

habitat.use.note: EltonTraits ForStrat-ground 20; ForStrat-understory 40 + ForStrat-midhigh 40 (80) mapped to arboreal.

habitat.shelter_tag.note: Authored: the winter roost is 'in trees in secluded swamps or dense vegetation' and the nest is usually in a dense bush, so shrub_thicket; the source describes the roost shelter directly but not as a resource tag.

habitat.resources.note: Food weights follow traits.diet. Nesting weight 1.0 on nest_cup follows the nest description. Perch and shrub_thicket shelter weights are authored judgement; no open source quantifies their relative use.

habitat.human_tolerance.note: 'The breeding habitat is woodland and more open farmland and urban areas', 'The species is not shy about nesting close to human habitations', and the species is described as the most abundant landbird in North America at about 370 million individuals; light_max is authored (judgement).

seasonal.strategy.note: 'While robins occasionally overwinter in the northern part of the United States and southern Canada, most migrate to winter south of Canada from Florida and the Gulf Coast to central Mexico, as well as along the Pacific Coast. Most depart south by the end of August and begin to return north in February and March.'

seasonal.winter_fraction.note: Judgement: the source says most of the population winters south of Canada and that robins only 'occasionally overwinter' in the northern US and southern Canada, without giving a proportion, so 0.1 is an authored figure for the share remaining on the northern breeding grounds.

seasonal.phases.note: Breeding window from 'beginning to breed shortly after returning to its summer range' with a February-March return and the late-February song start, plus the 14-day incubation and two-week nestling period; winter flocking from the communal-roost and day-flocking description; the US-WV regional phase is a judgement from the stated overwintering range and is labelled as such in its own note.

seasonal.life_stages.note: Juvenile duration from the 14-day incubation plus the two weeks to leave the nest and 'juveniles become capable of sustained flight two weeks after fledging' (42 days used); 'Chicks become sexually mature at one year of age' supports the adult stage. Scale is authored judgement and the egg stage carries no duration because none is sourced.

vocalizations.song.note: From the Vocalization section, including the season 'from late February or early March to late July or early August' and the habit of singing from a high perch, often before dawn.

vocalizations.alarm.note: The source describes calls 'used for communicating specific information, such as when a ground predator approaches and when a nest or another American robin is being directly threatened' but does not name or describe a specific alarm call, so the description is an authored summary of those two contexts and no attempt is made to render the call itself.

vocalizations.note: Contexts from the Vocalization and Behavior sections; months, time windows and cooldowns are authored judgement, since no open source quantifies them. No open source gives frequency bands, so freq_hz is omitted.

look.note: Colours from the Description section (head varying from jet black to grey with white eye arcs and supercilia, white throat with black streaks, white belly and undertail coverts, brown back, reddish-orange breast from rich red maroon to peachy orange, mainly yellow bill with a variably dark tip, brown legs and feet). The breast is coloured from the markings slot and the head from the accent slot to render the dark hood against the orange breast; proportions are authored judgement for a long-legged, upright thrush.

behavior.note: Authored parameters for the shared perching-songbird program. food_tag set to invertebrate, matching the ground-foraging behaviour the program implements; flee_m raised to 8 m for a larger, more alert bird than the program's default; nest_m1/nest_m2 widened to March-August to cover repeated broods on a new nest each time.
